passage:
Saturday. Over tea, her mother Maria said, "I was too hard on you for years. I am sorry." Dilnaz waited for relief. What came instead was heat in her chest. "Why now?" she said, and left the table.

Tuesday. Dilnaz told a friend, "Shouldn't I be relieved? I am furious." The friend said, "It has been years. Both can be true." Dilnaz slept badly and did not answer Maria's morning text.

The next Sunday. Dilnaz called Maria. "I heard you. I am not ready to say it is fine. But I could see you meant it." They talked for ten minutes about groceries and the weather. It was small. It was something.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz say before leaving the table?
Why did Dilnaz feel anger rather than relief?
qa.a: Years of hurt had built up, so the apology stirred anger, and she was not ready to call it fine.

qa.q: How can trust rebuild after an apology like this?
qa.a: Through steady, consistent behaviour over time, starting with small talks like groceries and the weather, without forcing forgiveness.

qa.q: How might Maria have felt when Dilnaz did not answer the morning text?
qa.a: Maria may have felt anxious or hurt, but Dilnaz's later call let Maria see the apology had been heard.

grounding: A parent finally apologises and the protagonist feels anger, not relief; she takes time, accepts what is sincere and lets trust rebuild slowly.

passage:
Counselling note, Thursday.
Ankita arrived early and did not sit down for several minutes. She said her mother, Indu, phoned on Sunday and apologised for the years Ankita was sent to her uncle's house "to be less trouble". Ankita expected to feel relieved. Instead she felt furious, "like the anger had been waiting in a cupboard". She asked whether that made her ungrateful. I told her that anger after a long-awaited apology is common and does not cancel the apology. We talked about which parts of Indu's words felt sincere to her: the specific mention of the uncle's house did; the line "anyway, it's in the past" did not. She decided to reply by message, not a call, and to watch whether the weekly check-ins Indu offered actually happen.
Next session: review how the first two check-ins went.

qa.q: How did Ankita decide to reply to her mother?
What did Ankita feel after the apology, and why did it surprise her?
qa.a: She felt furious rather than relieved, and worried the anger made her ungrateful, because she had expected relief.

qa.q: How does the counsellor help Ankita take the apology at her own pace?
qa.a: The counsellor says the anger is common, helps her sort sincere parts from hollow ones, and supports her plan to watch whether the weekly check-ins happen.

qa.q: What might Indu hope for after making the call?
qa.a: Indu may hope the apology mends things quickly and could feel anxious at a reply by message; trust now depends on keeping the weekly check-ins.

grounding: A parent apologises after many years and the adult child feels unexpected anger, then takes time and lets trust rest on consistent behaviour.

passage:
Hemant's diary, 12 Nov, night.
Papa said sorry today. Eleven years late, at Jahnavi's engagement, next to the sweets counter, like it was a small thing. "I was wrong to throw your books out. I was wrong about a lot."
I wanted to feel happy. Everyone around us was smiling. Instead my ears went hot and I walked out to the parking lot and kicked a tyre. Who apologises next to the gulab jamuns??
Jahnavi found me there. She didn't say calm down. She just stood with me.
Okay. Writing it out. He did say the words, and his voice cracked, so maybe some of it was real. I don't have to decide tonight. He said he'd come to my flat on Sunday to help fix the shelf. If he actually comes, that will mean more than the sorry.
Still angry. That's allowed.

qa.q: Where was Papa standing when he apologised?
qa.a: Next to the sweets counter at Jahnavi's engagement.

qa.q: Why did Hemant walk out to the parking lot?
qa.a: Hemant felt a rush of anger instead of happiness, ears hot, because the apology came eleven years late and so casually in a crowd.

qa.q: What will show Hemant whether Papa's apology was sincere?
qa.a: Whether Papa actually comes on Sunday to help fix the shelf; steady actions will mean more than the words.

qa.q: How might Papa feel after Hemant walks out?
qa.a: Papa may feel ashamed and worried the apology failed, though his cracked voice suggests he meant it; Sunday is his chance to show it.

grounding: A parent apologises after years and the protagonist feels anger rather than relief, then lets trust depend on consistent behaviour.
